analysis.one_liner: Directs the FDA to set and enforce limits on toxic heavy metals like lead and arsenic in baby food, pouches, and juice.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2024 and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 would have required the FDA to set binding limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in food made for babies and toddlers, in fruit-and-vegetable pouches, and in juice. It would have required companies to test their finished products at accredited labs, keep the results open to FDA inspection, run environmental monitoring in their plants, and face mandatory recall if their baby food exceeded the limits. It was introduced by Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi with two cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and babies would gain: enforceable federal limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in food made for children under two, plus regular testing companies must perform and open to FDA inspection, and FDA power to force a recall of contaminated baby food.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the FDA to set legally enforceable limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food, fruit-and-vegetable pouches, and juice.
It requires makers of these foods to regularly sample and test final products at accredited labs, keep records open to FDA inspection, and run environmental monitoring programs in their plants.

It lets the FDA order a mandatory recall of contaminated baby and toddler food — currently infant food is largely exempt from that authority — and lets FDA request company records in lieu of an inspection.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of baby food, toddler food, juice, and fruit-and-vegetable pouches would bear the cost of testing, sampling plans, environmental monitoring, and records, and could face recalls or adulteration findings if their products exceed the limits.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local governments from setting their own contaminant limits, testing, or labeling requirements for these foods, so no state could go further than the federal limits.

Compliance costs — routine accredited-laboratory testing, recordkeeping, and environmental monitoring — fall on food manufacturers and could raise prices for baby and toddler foods, and FDA's own sampling program would require new agency capacity.

Limits are set through FDA administrative orders with a phased schedule (lead and arsenic by late 2025, cadmium by 2026, mercury by 2028) and take into account the extent to which contamination 'cannot be avoided,' which could yield limits weaker than advocates want.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — enforceable limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in food aimed at babies, with testing and mandatory recall authority — are significant and relatively cheap to achieve, since the costs fall on manufacturers' testing and recordkeeping. The main drawbacks are compliance costs that could raise prices modestly and a preemption clause that locks states out of setting tougher rules, making the federal limits the ceiling as well as the floor. Even so, the bill would have given families protection they currently lack.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, which kills any bill not passed by both chambers.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 14, 2024, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of baby food, juice, and fruit-and-vegetable pouches benefit, because they avoid binding federal limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in their products. Parents and babies are left with the status quo: federal guidance and voluntary industry testing, but no enforceable limits.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Oversight Subcommittee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
for.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on record; it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill imposes binding contaminant limits, mandatory testing, environmental monitoring, recordkeeping, and expanded recall exposure on makers of food for children under two. That cost lands on an industry whose products carry heavy metals to babies.
Juice and puree pouches would face the same limits and testing requirements, since they are significant sources of children's heavy metal exposure.
